script.opening: "This is so embarrassing — I’ve got these really painful blisters and sores down below, it stings terribly when I wee, and I feel fluey and achy. I looked it up and I’m terrified it’s herpes. Does that mean I’m dirty? Will I have this forever? What do I tell my partner?"

facts.text: Started 3 days ago as tingling, then little blisters on both sides of the vulva, now some have burst into raw shallow sores. More today than yesterday. Very painful to sit or walk. Lumps in both groins, tender.
Stings terribly; she’s been putting off going. Can still pass urine — went 3 hours ago. If asked: has not tried passing urine in a warm bath.
Fluey, achy, temperature 38.1 on her own thermometer last night. No headache with a stiff neck, no light sensitivity. No rash anywhere else.

One partner, Ben, for 8 months; they stopped using condoms after 2 months. Oral sex as well. He has never mentioned cold sores or genital sores, but she has seen him with a cold sore once. One previous partner, 2 years ago. Never had an STI test.
On the combined pill, takes it reliably. Last period 2 weeks ago. Doesn’t think she could be pregnant.
Well otherwise, no medicines apart from the pill, no allergies. Never had anything like this before. Never had cold sores herself.
Primary school teaching assistant. Lives with a flatmate. Hasn’t told Ben yet; he’s away this week.

Mortified and tearful, avoiding the camera at first. You use words like "dirty" and "forever". Relax noticeably if the doctor is matter-of-fact and non-judgemental and explains how common it is. Ask: "What if he thinks I cheated?" If the doctor asks to see the area on video, you are uncomfortable and would prefer to send a photo or be seen in person with a chaperone.

ice.ideas: "It’s herpes. I looked it up. It means I’m dirty."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her relationship: "What if he thinks I cheated? Or did he cheat on me?" Also fears never being able to have children normally, and having it "forever".
ice.expectations: "Something to make it stop hurting, and to know what this means for me and Ben."

checkpoints.text: Recognises FIRST-EPISODE GENITAL HERPES (painful grouped vesicles/ulcers, dysuria, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, flu-like systemic symptoms) and considers other causes of genital ulceration

Confirms appropriately — clinical diagnosis supported by an HSV swab/PCR from a lesion — and involves/refers GUM/sexual-health services for confirmation, full STI screen (including HIV and syphilis) and support with telling partners

Treats promptly with an oral ANTIVIRAL (aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days, BASHH 2024; valaciclovir/famciclovir alternatives) started early without waiting for the swab, asks about possible pregnancy, plus symptomatic care (analgesia, saline bathing, topical anaesthetic, fluids) and warns about URINARY RETENTION
Counsels the NATURAL HISTORY in a destigmatising way — common, manageable, lifelong but recurrences usually milder/shorter and often less frequent; not "dirty"/promiscuous

Counsels TRANSMISSION and risk reduction (asymptomatic shedding, condoms, partner disclosure, suppressive therapy for frequent recurrences) and the importance of disclosing herpes in any future PREGNANCY (neonatal risk)
Leads with COMPASSION — explicitly addressing the shame and the "dirty/forever/partner" fears — rather than a brisk prescription, and validates her distress
Explains the diagnosis and plan clearly, checks understanding, and supports her through a distressing diagnosis

Safety-nets and follows up: urinary retention/severe symptoms → urgent review, GUM referral and STI-screen follow-up, recurrence and suppression discussion, pregnancy advice, and review — accurate treatment + destigmatising counselling

worked.txt: "First, please don’t be embarrassed, and let me say this clearly: this does NOT mean you’re ‘dirty’ — genital herpes is extremely common and very manageable. I can see you’re in pain and frightened, so let’s sort both the symptoms and your worries."

"It does look like a first episode of herpes. I’d like to see you in person today, with a chaperone if you’d like one, to examine you and take a swab from a sore to confirm it — could you be pregnant at the moment? I’d also like you to be seen at the sexual-health clinic for a full check, including HIV and syphilis tests, and to help with telling partners — they’re experts and completely confidential."

"I’ll start you on an antiviral tablet today, without waiting for the swab — aciclovir three times a day for five days — it works best started early and will settle this episode faster. For the pain: salt-water baths, painkillers, and a numbing gel for weeing, plus plenty of fluids. Passing urine in a warm bath can help. If it becomes so sore you can’t pass urine at all, contact us urgently — that occasionally needs hospital."

"Honestly: the virus does stay in the body, so it can come back — but here’s the reassuring part: recurrences are usually much milder and shorter than this first one, and often become less frequent over time. If they’re frequent, a daily tablet can suppress them."

"On your partner — it can pass on even without visible sores, so condoms help reduce, though not remove, the risk. It’s worth an honest conversation; the clinic can help with that. None of this makes you a bad person."

"One important thing for the future: if you’re ever pregnant, tell your midwife/doctor you’ve had herpes, as it needs specific care to protect the baby. Come back if it worsens, you can’t pass urine, or you’re struggling with how you feel about it — that matters too."

f.learning: A FIRST EPISODE of genital herpes (HSV) presents with PAINFUL grouped VESICLES progressing to shallow ULCERS on the genitals, DYSURIA, tender INGUINAL lymphadenopathy and flu-like SYSTEMIC symptoms — first episodes being more painful and systemic than recurrences — and should be distinguished from other causes of genital ulceration (other STIs, aphthous/Behçet’s, fixed drug eruption). Diagnosis is clinical after a chaperoned face-to-face examination, supported by an HSV SWAB/PCR from the base of a lesion (BASHH 2024), and GUM/sexual-health services should ideally be involved for confirmation, a FULL STI screen including HIV and syphilis, support with telling partners (BASHH 2024: partner notification is not required as a public health measure, but telling partners is recommended) and expert counselling. Treat promptly with an oral ANTIVIRAL without waiting for the swab (BASHH 2024: within 5 days of onset or while new lesions form; aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days preferred, valaciclovir/famciclovir alternatives, dose per BNF), most effective started EARLY in a first episode, plus symptomatic care (analgesia, saline bathing, topical anaesthetic for dysuria, fluids), warning about URINARY RETENTION from severe dysuria (occasionally needing admission/catheter — the suprapubic route is considered) and advising against sexual contact while lesions are present. Critically, lead with compassionate, DESTIGMATISING counselling: genital herpes is COMMON and MANAGEABLE, a lifelong infection (the virus persists) but with RECURRENCES that are usually MILDER and SHORTER and often less frequent over time, and it does NOT mean the patient is "dirty" or promiscuous — directly addressing shame and the "forever" fear. Counsel transmission and risk reduction (asymptomatic SHEDDING means transmission can occur without lesions; condoms reduce but do not eliminate risk; partner disclosure; SUPPRESSIVE antiviral therapy for frequent recurrences and to reduce transmission) and — after asking whether she could be pregnant now — the importance of disclosing a herpes history in any future PREGNANCY because of neonatal-herpes implications (BASHH/RCOG 2024). The hidden agenda is shame and fear about relationships and the future; the skill is accurate diagnosis and early antivirals AND compassionate destigmatising counselling with GUM involvement — not a brisk prescription.

knowledge.guideline: [1] BASHH UK national guideline for the management of anogenital herpes (2024) · [2] BASHH/RCOG Management of genital herpes in pregnancy and the neonate (2024 update) · [3] BASHH summary guidance on testing for sexually transmitted infections (2023) · [4] BHIVA/BASHH/BIA Adult HIV testing guidelines (2020)
knowledge.summary: Painful grouped blisters and shallow ulcers on the vulva with dysuria, tender groin nodes and flu-like illness is a first episode of genital herpes until proven otherwise. The GP should examine, take a lesion swab for HSV PCR, start aciclovir without waiting for the result, give symptom relief and warn about urinary retention, arrange a full STI screen through sexual health services, and spend real time on the shame, the “forever” question, partners and future pregnancy.

points.t: First episodes are usually the most severe: multiple painful vesicles that break into shallow ulcers, dysuria, tender inguinal nodes, fever and myalgia. Consider other causes of genital ulcers: syphilis (usually painless), trauma, aphthous or Behçet’s ulcers, fixed drug eruption and, if persistent, vulval cancer.

BASHH [1]: take a swab from the base of a lesion for HSV PCR, which also types HSV-1 or HSV-2. Offer a full STI screen including chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV [3][4], ideally through a sexual health clinic; repeat syphilis and HIV tests if still in the window period.

BASHH [1]: start oral antiviral within 5 days of onset or while new lesions are still forming; do not wait for the swab result. Aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days is preferred; valaciclovir and famciclovir are alternatives (dose per BNF). Review at 5 days and continue if new lesions are still appearing.

BASHH [1]: saline bathing, simple analgesia, and topical 5% lidocaine or petroleum jelly. Passing urine in a warm bath or with water poured over the area eases dysuria. Urinary retention can occur; if catheterisation is needed, the suprapubic route is considered. Avoid sex until lesions have healed.

The virus stays in the body, but recurrences are usually milder and shorter than a first episode, especially with HSV-1. Transmission can happen without symptoms (asymptomatic shedding); condoms and suppressive antivirals reduce but do not remove the risk. BASHH [1]: partner notification is not required as a public health measure, but telling partners is recommended. Suppressive treatment is considered for frequent recurrences (trials used 6 or more a year).

BASHH/RCOG [2]: she should tell her midwife or obstetrician about herpes in any future pregnancy. Recurrent herpes carries a low risk to the baby; a first episode in the third trimester carries the highest risk and changes delivery planning. Ask about possible current pregnancy now.

model.text: Hello Miss Hicks, I’m Dr Clarke. Take your time. What’s been happening?

This is so embarrassing. I’ve got these really painful blisters and sores down below, it stings terribly when I wee, and I feel fluey and achy. I looked it up and I’m terrified it’s herpes. Does that mean I’m dirty? Will I have this forever? What do I tell my partner?

Thank you for coming in. There’s nothing to be embarrassed about with me, and no, it wouldn’t mean you’re dirty. Those are really important questions and I promise we’ll answer each one. First, can I ask a few things about the symptoms?
model.why: Reassures on the “dirty” fear early; agrees the agenda

model.text: When did the sores start, and are new ones still appearing?
Three days ago. There are more today than yesterday.
Are you managing to pass urine, even though it stings?
Yes, but I’m putting it off because it’s so painful.
Any discharge, headache with a stiff neck, or pain in your back passage?
No. Just the sores and feeling rubbish.
Have you had anything like this before, around your mouth or genitals?
Never.
Could you be pregnant at the moment? And do you have any allergies to medicines?
I don’t think so. No allergies.
Can I ask about your partner? Is it a regular partner, and do you use condoms?
He’s my regular partner. I don’t know if he’s ever had anything like this.
You mentioned three fears: being dirty, having it forever, and what to tell him. Which is weighing on you most?
Him. What if he thinks I cheated? And the forever bit.
I’d like to examine you, with a chaperone, and take a swab from one of the sores to confirm what it is. Is that all right?
model.why: Consent, chaperone, swab for HSV PCR

model.text: Okay.

(After examination.) There are clusters of small blisters and shallow ulcers on the vulva, and tender glands in your groin. This fits a first episode of genital herpes. The swab will confirm it and tell us the type.

I’ll start you on an antiviral tablet today called aciclovir, three times a day for five days. It works best started early, and we don’t need to wait for the swab. For the pain: salt-water bathing, regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, and an anaesthetic gel. Passing urine in a warm bath really helps.
model.why: Aciclovir 400 mg TDS for 5 days (BASHH 2024); symptom relief

model.text: If you can’t pass urine at all, or it becomes very difficult, contact us or go to urgent care straight away, because that sometimes needs treatment in hospital.
And the forever part?

Honestly, the virus stays in the body. But the first episode is almost always the worst. Many people have few or no further outbreaks, and when they happen they’re usually milder and shorter. If they became frequent, a daily tablet can stop most of them.

About your partner: herpes is very common and many people carry it without ever knowing. It can be caught from someone without sores, so this doesn’t tell us anyone cheated. It can’t be dated like that. The sexual health clinic can talk it through with both of you. I’d suggest no sex until the sores have healed, and condoms after that help reduce the risk.
That helps. I thought it meant he’d been with someone.

I’d also like you to have a full check for other infections, including HIV and syphilis, at the sexual health clinic. And one thing for the future: if you’re ever pregnant, tell your midwife you’ve had herpes, because it helps them plan to keep the baby safe.
Can you tell me the main things you’ll do when you get home?
Tablets three times a day, salt baths, wee in the bath, clinic for tests, and call if I can’t wee.

Perfect. I’ll ring you with the swab result. Come back if it isn’t settling after five days, if you get a severe headache or stiff neck, or if you’re struggling with how you feel about it. That matters too.

social.t: Shame about herpes often outweighs the physical symptoms. Plain, non-judgemental language and accurate facts reduce it.
Fear of blame is common. Explaining asymptomatic carriage helps couples talk; sexual health clinics can support that conversation.

legal.t: Sexual health information is confidential. Sexual health clinics offer open access and confidential testing.
GMC guidance on intimate examinations and chaperones: offer a chaperone for an intimate examination and record the offer, whether it was accepted and who was present.

professional.t: Explain what the examination and swab involve and obtain consent before starting.
Record onset date, lesion description, swab taken, antiviral started, STI screen arranged and counselling given.

community.t: Offer referral for a full STI screen, typing results, partner discussions and ongoing advice about recurrences. Patient charities for herpes provide reliable information and support.

Aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days, started today (BASHH 2024)

pitfalls.intro: The treatment here is straightforward. The marks are in the examination and swab, the retention warning, and how well the candidate handles shame and the partner question.

items.fail: Waiting for the swab before starting treatment.
items.why: BASHH 2024 advises starting within 5 days or while new lesions form.
items.fix: Swab and start aciclovir the same day.

items.why: Other infections, including HIV and syphilis, can coexist.
items.fix: Arrange a full screen through sexual health services.

items.why: Severe dysuria can cause retention needing hospital care.
items.fix: Advise passing urine in the bath and urgent review if unable to pass it.

items.fail: Not asking about pregnancy or giving future pregnancy advice.
items.why: A first episode in late pregnancy changes delivery planning (BASHH/RCOG 2024).
items.fix: Ask now and advise telling the midwife in future.

items.fail: Implying her partner was unfaithful, or ignoring the question.
items.why: Asymptomatic carriage means infection cannot be dated.
items.fix: Explain this plainly and offer clinic support for the conversation.

items.why: It leaves her more frightened than necessary.
items.fix: Explain that recurrences are milder and can be suppressed.

timeMap.d: Let her ask her three questions. Say early that this doesn’t make her dirty, and promise to answer each.
Onset, new lesions, passing urine, previous episodes, pregnancy, allergy, sexual history.
Prioritise her fears. Chaperoned examination and HSV PCR swab.
Aciclovir now; symptom relief; retention warning; the “forever” answer.
Transmission and disclosure without blame; STI screen; future pregnancy; teach-back; safety-net.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes aciclovir briskly and ends; never examines or swabs; no STI screen; ignores the shame and partner questions; no retention warning.
wordPics.pass: Recognises first-episode herpes, swabs, starts aciclovir, gives symptom advice, refers for STI screening and answers her questions.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: addresses “dirty” in the first minute; checks the antiviral window and pregnancy status; explains that herpes cannot be dated so it does not imply infidelity; gives honest, hopeful natural history; advises on disclosure and condoms; warns about retention; mentions future pregnancy; confirms the plan by teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Well, it’s sexually transmitted, so your partner must have given it to you.”
avoid.instead: “Many people carry herpes without ever knowing, so this doesn’t tell us when or from whom.”
avoid.why: Blame is inaccurate and can harm relationships; asymptomatic carriage is common.

avoid.instead: “The virus stays in the body, but this first episode is usually the worst, and later ones are milder and can be prevented with tablets.”
avoid.why: True but bleak framing deepens distress; the balanced version is equally honest.

avoid.dont: “Let’s wait for the swab before treating.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll start the antiviral today; it works best early.”
avoid.why: BASHH advises treating a first episode within 5 days or while new lesions form, without waiting.

Picked up “What do I tell my partner?” and addressed the fear of infidelity.
Idea (herpes, from looking it up), concerns (dirty, forever, partner), expectation (treatment and answers).
Chaperoned examination; lesion swab for HSV PCR; full STI screen including HIV and syphilis via sexual health.
First-episode HSV versus syphilis, other ulcer causes, and recurrence versus first episode.
Urinary retention, neurological symptoms and possible pregnancy screened.
Named a first episode of genital herpes, pending swab confirmation.
Aciclovir started without waiting for results (BASHH 2024); saline bathing, analgesia, topical anaesthetic.
Shame, partner disclosure and emotional impact addressed; sex avoided until healed.
Result call; review if not settling; retention and neurological safety-net; future pregnancy advice.

social.t: Shame about herpes often outweighs the physical symptoms. Plain, non-judgemental language and accurate facts reduce it.
Fear of blame is common. Explaining asymptomatic carriage helps couples talk; sexual health clinics can support that conversation.

legal.t: Sexual health information is confidential. Sexual health clinics offer open access and confidential testing.
GMC guidance on intimate examinations and chaperones: offer a chaperone for an intimate examination and record the offer, whether it was accepted and who was present.

professional.t: Explain what the examination and swab involve and obtain consent before starting.
Record onset date, lesion description, swab taken, antiviral started, STI screen arranged and counselling given.

community.t: Offer referral for a full STI screen, typing results, partner discussions and ongoing advice about recurrences. Patient charities for herpes provide reliable information and support.

redFlags: Severe headache, neck stiffness or photophobia (meningism)
Painless ulcer (syphilis) or persistent ulcer (other causes)
psychosocial: Fear her partner will think she cheated
Worry about the future and relationships
ice: Idea: herpes, from looking it up
Concern: being dirty; having it forever; telling her partner

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This looks like a first episode of genital herpes. The swab will confirm it and tell us the type.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Herpes is a very common virus. After the first outbreak it rests quietly in the nerves and can occasionally cause a milder flare. Many people carry it without ever knowing.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if this makes you dirty: it doesn’t. You asked if it’s forever: the virus stays, but this is usually the worst it gets.”
management.psychosocial: Defuse blame; support disclosure; offer the sexual health clinic for joint conversations; acknowledge the emotional impact.
sharedPlan: Lesion swab for HSV PCR; full STI screen including HIV and syphilis
Aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days, started today (BASHH 2024)
Saline bathing, analgesia, topical lidocaine; no sex until healed; condoms afterwards
safetyNet: Cannot pass urine: urgent same-day review
Severe headache or stiff neck: urgent review
Tell the midwife about herpes in any future pregnancy (BASHH/RCOG 2024)

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The treatment here is straightforward. The marks are in the examination and swab, the retention warning, and how well the candidate handles shame and the partner question.

items.fail: Waiting for the swab before starting treatment.
items.why: BASHH 2024 advises starting within 5 days or while new lesions form.
items.fix: Swab and start aciclovir the same day.

items.why: Other infections, including HIV and syphilis, can coexist.
items.fix: Arrange a full screen through sexual health services.

items.why: Severe dysuria can cause retention needing hospital care.
items.fix: Advise passing urine in the bath and urgent review if unable to pass it.

items.fail: Not asking about pregnancy or giving future pregnancy advice.
items.why: A first episode in late pregnancy changes delivery planning (BASHH/RCOG 2024).
items.fix: Ask now and advise telling the midwife in future.

items.fail: Implying her partner was unfaithful, or ignoring the question.
items.why: Asymptomatic carriage means infection cannot be dated.
items.fix: Explain this plainly and offer clinic support for the conversation.

items.why: It leaves her more frightened than necessary.
items.fix: Explain that recurrences are milder and can be suppressed.
